name: Security Concepts
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Tell threats, vulnerabilities and exploits apart, recognize common network attacks and pick the mitigation for each.

lesson.intro: Every security feature in the CCNA (ACLs, port security, DHCP snooping, VPNs, AAA, WPA3) exists to stop a specific attack. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, the attacker's playbook, the human side of security, and a map from each attack to its control.
objectives: Distinguish vulnerability, exploit, threat and mitigation, and rank risk
Explain spoofing, DoS, DDoS, reflection, amplification and MITM attacks
Classify reconnaissance, malware, social engineering and password attacks
Describe user awareness, user training and physical access control
Match each common attack to the control that mitigates it

sections.title: Vulnerability, exploit, threat, mitigation
sections.key: A vulnerability is a weakness, an exploit is the tool that abuses it, a threat is someone able and willing to use it, and a mitigation reduces the risk.
sections.body:
A branch switch runs an old image with a published bug in its web interface, and that interface is reachable from the guest Wi-Fi. Nothing bad has happened yet. Is the network at risk? Security people answer with four precise words.

[[visual]]

Vulnerabilities exist in every network all the time. They become a threat when someone has an exploit plus access. Most Domain 5 configuration either removes vulnerabilities (patches, SSH instead of Telnet) or removes access (ACLs, VPNs).

An **asset** is whatever you protect. A **zero-day** is a vulnerability attackers know, and may already exploit, before the vendor has a fix. Until then only other layers help: filtering who can reach the service, segmentation and monitoring.

visual.title: Four words, one scenario
rows: A weakness that could compromise security
The web interface bug; also a default password or an unlocked closet
A tool or technique that abuses a specific vulnerability
A script that sends the malformed request the bug mishandles
Someone (or malware) with an exploit plus the intent and opportunity to use it
An attacker on the guest Wi-Fi who has the script
Patching, disabling the HTTP server, an ACL blocking guests
A better lock, an alarm, a guard

sections.tip: Read exam scenarios for the noun: a weakness is a vulnerability, a tool is an exploit, an actor with intent is a threat, a fix is a mitigation.
sections.pitfall: Calling a vulnerability a threat. The weakness exists even when nobody is attacking; it only becomes a threat when someone has the means and intent to exploit it.

check.question: A router's software has a publicly documented flaw, but no attack code exists for it yet. What is the flaw?
choices: A threat
An exploit
A vulnerability
A mitigation
check.explanation: The flaw is a weakness, which makes it a vulnerability. An exploit would be the code that abuses it, and a threat needs someone with that exploit and the intent to use it.

sections.title: Risk, the CIA triad and defense in depth
sections.key: Rank risk by likelihood and impact, describe impact as lost confidentiality, integrity or availability, and layer controls so one failure is not fatal.
sections.body:
Teams cannot fix everything at once, so they rank by **risk**: how likely a threat is to succeed, combined with the damage it would do. An internet-facing VPN gateway with a default password is high on both; an isolated lab switch is low. A patch or ACL lowers likelihood; an offline backup lowers impact.

[[visual]]

Three principles lower risk everywhere:

- **Attack surface**: every open port, service, account, wall jack and wireless network. Shrink it by disabling what you do not use.
- **Least privilege**: only the access each role needs. The help desk gets show commands, not configuration; guests reach the internet, not servers.
- **Segmentation**: VLANs, ACLs and firewalls, so one compromised host cannot reach everything.

No control is perfect, so networks layer them. That is **defense in depth**: if one layer fails, the next still stands.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Confidentiality
points: Only authorized people can read the data
Broken by an eavesdropper capturing Telnet passwords

items.title: Integrity
points: Data is not changed without detection
Broken by a man in the middle editing a payment

items.title: Availability
points: Users can reach the service when they need it

layers.label: Physical
layers.detail: Badge readers, locked closets: stop console access and theft

layers.label: Human
layers.detail: Awareness, training, MFA: stop phishing and social engineering

layers.label: Edge
layers.detail: ACLs, firewalls, IPS: stop scans, spoofing, known exploits

layers.label: Access
layers.detail: Port security, DHCP snooping, DAI: stop rogue devices and ARP poisoning

layers.label: Device
layers.detail: Hashed secrets, SSH, AAA: stop password guessing

layers.label: Data
layers.detail: IPsec, TLS, WPA3: stop eavesdropping and tampering

sections.pitfall: Treating one strong control as enough. A firewall does nothing against a phished password used from inside the network, which is why exam answers favor layered mitigations.

check.question: A firewall blocks every inbound connection from the internet, so a manager proposes to stop patching the internal servers. Which principle argues most directly against this?
choices: Least privilege
Defense in depth
Availability
Reconnaissance
check.explanation: Defense in depth assumes any single layer can fail or be bypassed (a phished laptop inside, a misconfigured rule), so patching still matters behind the firewall. Least privilege is about limiting access rights, not layering controls.

sections.title: Spoofing, denial of service and amplification
sections.key: Spoofing fakes a packet's source address; it powers SYN floods and reflection attacks, where the spoofed source is the victim who receives the replies.
sections.body:
Networks trust addresses: a packet with source 192.0.2.10 is assumed to come from 192.0.2.10. **Spoofing** writes a fake source IP or MAC address. It is rarely the goal; it powers the attacks below.

[[visual]]

In a **TCP SYN flood**, spoofed SYNs make the server answer with SYN-ACKs and hold half-open connections, waiting for ACKs that never come. Its table fills and real clients are refused.

[[visual 2]]

Mitigations: drop spoofed sources at the edge (inbound packets carrying your own or private addresses, outbound packets not carrying yours), close open resolvers, rate-limit, use firewall or IPS SYN protection, and buy upstream DDoS scrubbing.

[[code]]

visual.title: Floods and how they scale
rows: Exhausts bandwidth, CPU or a connection table: SYN, ICMP or UDP floods
Thousands of infected **bots**, ordered by a command-and-control server, hit one target
Blocking one source address does nothing
Requests carry the victim's spoofed address, so innocent **reflectors** reply to the victim
No packet carries the attacker's address
Reflection where a small request triggers a large reply: open DNS resolvers, old NTP servers

messages.label: Reply, 2,400 bytes
messages.detail: 40 times larger, to the spoofed source

messages.note: Repeat through thousands of resolvers: the victim is flooded

sections.code:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended OUTSIDE-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# remark Private sources never arrive from the internet
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 172.16.0.0 0.15.255.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 192.168.0.0 0.0.255.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group OUTSIDE-IN in
sections.pitfall: Mixing up the reflector and the target. The reflector is an innocent middleman answering what looks like a normal request; the target is whoever owns the spoofed source address.

activity.title: Where a SYN flood bites
activity.prompt: Step through a normal handshake, then the lost-segment case. Notice that after SYN and SYN-ACK the server is holding state while it waits for the final ACK. Now picture thousands of SYNs from spoofed addresses whose ACK never arrives: that waiting state is what a SYN flood multiplies until the server's table is full.

check.question: In a reflection attack, which address does the attacker place in the source field of the requests it sends?
choices: Its own real address
The reflector's address
A broadcast address
The target's address
check.explanation: The attacker spoofs the target's address so that every reply from the reflector is sent to the target. Using its own address would just send the replies back to the attacker.

sections.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks
sections.key: A man in the middle silently relays traffic between victims to read or change it; on a LAN it gets there with ARP poisoning or a rogue DHCP server.
sections.body:
Some attackers do not want to break anything. They want to sit between two devices and read or change what passes: a **man-in-the-middle (MITM)** attack.

Hosts trust ARP replies blindly, even unrequested **gratuitous ARP**. That makes **ARP poisoning** easy:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A **rogue DHCP server** does the same job: it answers Discovers first and hands out the attacker's IP as the default gateway. On Wi-Fi, an **evil twin** access point copies a real SSID.

In the middle, the attacker can eavesdrop (confidentiality) or modify data (integrity). Defend in two layers: **Dynamic ARP Inspection** and **DHCP snooping** on switches, and **encryption** (TLS, SSH, IPsec) so intercepted data is unreadable and tampering shows.

messages.note: Traffic still works, so the victim notices nothing

visual.title: PC1's ARP cache after poisoning
visual.caption: Two IPs on one MAC, one of them the gateway's, is the signature of ARP poisoning.

sections.pitfall: Assuming a MITM attack breaks the connection. A skilled attacker forwards everything onward so the victim's applications keep working; the absence of symptoms is the point.

activity.title: Watch ARP do its job
activity.prompt: Step through the journey and pause at the ARP step. The sender caches whatever reply arrives; nothing in ARP proves the reply came from the real owner of the IP address. Ask yourself what would happen if a different host answered first, or kept answering. That gap is what ARP poisoning exploits.

check.question: After poisoning ARP caches, why does the attacker forward the victims' packets on to the real gateway?
choices: ARP requires every reply to be forwarded
So the victims' traffic keeps working and the interception goes unnoticed
To refresh the switch's MAC address table
Because the attacker cannot drop packets once in the path
check.explanation: If the attacker dropped the traffic, users would notice an outage. Forwarding keeps everything working while the attacker reads or alters the data in transit.

sections.title: Reconnaissance and buffer overflows
sections.key: Reconnaissance maps targets before an attack; a buffer overflow sends more data than a program's buffer holds, crashing it or running the attacker's code.
sections.body:
Before a serious attack, attackers scout. A **reconnaissance attack** gathers information so the real attack can be focused:

[[visual]]

Reconnaissance exploits nothing, so it is easy to dismiss. Do not: scans in a firewall or IPS log are an early warning. Expose only the services you need, filter unneeded ICMP and ports at the edge, and alert on scan patterns.

A **buffer overflow** targets a programming flaw. A program that does not check input length lets an attacker send more data than its fixed-size buffer holds, overwriting neighboring memory. At best the service crashes (a DoS); at worst it runs the attacker's own code.

The fix is patching: upgrade IOS when Cisco publishes an advisory. Until then, disable the service (`no ip http server`) or restrict it with an ACL.

steps.label: Public lookups
steps.detail: `whois`, `nslookup`, `dig`: who owns the domain and its address blocks

steps.label: Version detection
steps.detail: Port 80 runs an old, unpatched web server

steps.label: Exploit
steps.detail: Only now does the real attack start

sections.pitfall: Thinking a scan is harmless because nothing broke. Reconnaissance is the planning phase; treat it as a signal that someone is choosing targets.

check.question: An attacker pings every address in a /24, then probes the hosts that answered on TCP ports 1 to 1024. What kind of attack is this?
choices: Buffer overflow
Reconnaissance
Amplification
Man in the middle
check.explanation: A ping sweep followed by a port scan gathers information about live hosts and services. That is reconnaissance; nothing has been exploited yet.

sections.title: Malware
sections.key: Trojans, viruses and worms differ in how they spread: hidden in useful software, attached to other files, or copying themselves across the network unaided.
sections.body:
**Malware** is malicious software. The CCNA expects you to tell the classic three apart by how they spread.

[[visual]]

Other kinds are named by what they do: **ransomware** encrypts data and demands payment, **spyware** and **keyloggers** steal information, **bots** wait for command-and-control orders (as in a DDoS), and **rootkits** hide malware from the operating system.

Malware gets in through email, drive-by downloads, infected USB drives and unpatched services. A next-generation firewall or IPS matches traffic against signatures of known malware and drops it.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: The classic three
rows: Hidden inside software that looks useful, such as a free PDF converter
Injects itself into other programs or files, and spreads when they are copied or shared
Exploits a vulnerable network service and copies itself host to host
No: it spreads by itself, in minutes

visual.title: Mitigations
rows: Worms, which live on unpatched services
Limits what malware can do once inside
Slows a worm's spread between segments

sections.pitfall: Calling every piece of malware a virus. On the exam, the deciding question is how it spreads: hidden in software (trojan), attached to files (virus) or by itself (worm).

check.question: Malware spreads from server to server by exploiting an unpatched file-sharing service, with no user opening or running anything. Which type is it?
choices: Worm
Trojan horse
Virus
Spyware
check.explanation: Spreading by itself through a network vulnerability, with no user action, is the defining trait of a worm. Trojans and viruses both need a user to install, open or share something.

sections.title: Social engineering and phishing
sections.key: Social engineering attacks the person, not the system; phishing variants are named by their target (spear phishing, whaling) or their channel (vishing, smishing).
sections.body:
The easiest system to hack is often the person using it. **Social engineering** exploits trust and helpfulness: a caller claiming to be IT asks for a password, someone watches a PIN being typed (**shoulder surfing**), or a stranger follows an employee through a badge door (**tailgating**).

**Phishing** disguises a malicious link or attachment as something legitimate. The exam tests its variants by scenario:

[[visual]]

Mitigations are mostly human: awareness, training, verifying unusual requests through a second channel, and multifactor authentication so a phished password is not enough. Email filtering and secure DNS help too.

visual.title: Phishing and its relatives
rows: Email posing as a real company, with a fake login link or a malicious attachment
Tailored message to a specific group, such as one company's finance team
Aimed at executives and other high-profile people
Poisoned DNS or hosts file: even the correct URL leads to a fake site
Malware planted on a site the targets already visit
An invented story (an auditor, a new vendor) to justify an odd request
Infected USB drives left where curious people will plug them in

sections.pitfall: Confusing pharming with phishing. Phishing lures you with a fake link; pharming redirects you even when you type the real address.

check.question: Users type their bank's correct URL but land on a convincing fake site, because a DNS server was tampered with. What is this attack?
choices: Spear phishing
Whaling
Pharming
Smishing
check.explanation: Pharming corrupts name resolution so the correct name resolves to the attacker's address. No deceptive link was needed, which rules out the phishing variants.

sections.title: Password attacks
sections.key: Lockouts slow only online guessing; against stolen password hashes, what matters is password length and a slow, salted hash.
sections.body:
Usernames are easy to guess (often `admin`), so the password is usually the only barrier.

[[visual]]

Where the guessing happens matters:

[[visual 2]]

Stored passwords should be hashed with a **salt**: a random value stored with each hash, so two users with the same password get different hashes. Precomputed **rainbow tables** become useless, and each password must be cracked separately. A salt is not secret.

Length beats complexity, because every extra character multiplies the search space:

[[visual 3]]

Mitigations: long passphrases, no default or reused passwords, slow salted hashes, login rate limiting and multifactor authentication.

visual.title: Three ways to guess
rows: Obvious values: defaults like admin/admin or cisco/cisco, password123, the company name
Every entry in a word list, often millions of passwords leaked in earlier breaches
Every combination of characters: it always succeeds eventually, in seconds or in centuries

items.title: Online attack
points: Guesses typed into the real login prompt
Stopped by lockouts and login delays

items.title: Offline attack
points: First steals stored hashes, such as a configuration backup
Cracks them on the attacker's own hardware at billions of guesses per second

visual.title: Time to try every password at 10 billion guesses per second

sections.pitfall: Believing account lockout stops password cracking. Lockouts only slow online attacks; an offline attack on stolen hashes never touches the login prompt.

check.question: An attacker copies a configuration backup containing password hashes and cracks them on a GPU rig at home. What kind of attack is this?
choices: An online dictionary attack
A social engineering attack
A reconnaissance attack
An offline password attack
check.explanation: The guessing happens on the attacker's own hardware against stolen hashes, which makes it an offline attack. Login lockouts and delays on the device cannot slow it down.

sections.title: Security program elements
sections.key: The blueprint's three security program elements are user awareness (ongoing reminders), user training (formal courses on policy) and physical access control.
sections.body:
Firewalls cannot stop a user from reading a password over the phone, or a visitor from walking into an unlocked wiring closet. That is why the blueprint lists three **security program elements**: the human and physical layer.

[[visual]]

Physical access deserves respect. Anyone at a router's console can reboot it, run **password recovery** and take full control, however strong its passwords. A locked closet is a network control.

These elements sit inside a wider program: a written **security policy** for training to teach, an **incident response** plan, and regular **audits** that check the controls work.

items.title: User awareness
points: Everyone knows the threats aimed at them and how to report one
Reminders such as "IT never asks for your password", banners, a reporting address

items.title: User training
points: Required courses on the organization's written security policy
Simulated phishing with follow-up lessons for those who click

items.title: Physical access control
points: Locked closets and data centers, visitor escorts, cameras
Badge readers keep an audit trail and can be revoked instantly

sections.deeper:
**Incident response** usually runs in five steps: identify what happened, contain it (isolate the host or block the account), eradicate the cause, recover service, and learn from it so the policy and controls improve.

**Why badges beat keys.** Access can be granted per room and per person, every entry is logged, and a departing employee's badge is disabled in seconds. A metal key copied years ago keeps working until the lock is changed.
sections.pitfall: Treating awareness and training as the same thing. Awareness is continuous, informal reminding; training is scheduled, formal instruction on policy.

check.question: Why is physical access to a network closet treated as a serious security risk even when every device has strong passwords?
choices: Console access allows password recovery and full control of the device
Physical access lets an attacker read the passwords off the cables
Strong passwords only protect devices that are powered on
Switches send their passwords to any device plugged into them
check.explanation: With the console port and the ability to power-cycle a device, an attacker can run password recovery and reset the configuration's passwords. Passwords protect logins, not the hardware itself.

sections.title: Matching attacks to mitigations
sections.key: For any attack scenario, ask what it threatens (confidentiality, integrity or availability) and where it happens; the control that lives there is the answer.
sections.body:
Exam questions here describe an attack and ask for the control that stops it, or the reverse. The rest of Domain 5 is, in effect, this table:

[[visual]]

Two habits crack scenario questions. First, find the goal: reading data (confidentiality), changing it (integrity) or stopping service (availability). Second, find where it happens: the user, the access port, the wire, the device login or the internet edge. The control that lives there and protects that property is almost always the answer.

visual.title: Attack to control
rows: Inbound edge ACL denying your own and private ranges, plus outbound filtering
Hashed secrets, `login block-for`, a vty `access-class`, AAA with MFA
SSH instead of Telnet, SNMPv3 instead of v1 or v2c
Eavesdropping between sites or from hotels
Site-to-site IPsec VPN, TLS remote access VPN
Wireless eavesdropping, offline PSK cracking, forged deauthentication
WPA2 or WPA3 with AES, SAE and protected management frames
Patching, segmentation with ACLs, an IPS

sections.pitfall: Picking a control that works at the wrong place. Port security on the office switches does nothing for a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi; the VPN client on that laptop does.

check.question: Users keep finding that the MAC address listed for their default gateway in their ARP caches changes to an unknown device. Which control is designed to stop this attack?
choices: Port security
An IPsec VPN
Dynamic ARP Inspection
service password-encryption
check.explanation: Forged ARP replies that claim the gateway's IP are ARP poisoning, and Dynamic ARP Inspection drops ARP messages that do not match the switch's DHCP snooping bindings. Port security limits MAC addresses per port but does not inspect ARP contents.

keyTerms.definition: A weakness, such as a software bug, default password or unlocked closet, that could be used to compromise security.
A tool or technique that takes advantage of a specific vulnerability.
The real potential for harm: someone or something with an exploit and the intent and opportunity to use it.
Any action or control that reduces the likelihood or impact of an attack.
A vulnerability that attackers know about before the vendor has released a fix.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three properties an attack can break.
The sum of all points where an attacker could try to get in: services, ports, accounts, jacks and WLANs.
Giving each user, device and application only the access it needs to do its job.
Layering independent controls so that one failure does not expose the asset.
Faking a source IP or MAC address so packets appear to come from someone else.
Distributed denial of service: many compromised hosts (a botnet) flooding one target at once.
A reflection attack where small spoofed requests trigger much larger replies aimed at the victim.
An attack where the attacker sits in the path between two devices to read or change their traffic.
Information gathering, such as whois lookups, ping sweeps and port scans, before a real attack.
Malware that spreads by itself across the network by exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action.
A malicious message disguised as a legitimate one to steal credentials or deliver malware; variants include spear phishing, whaling, vishing and smishing.
Redirecting users to a fake site by compromising name resolution, even when they type the correct URL.
Trying every possible combination of characters until the password is found.

summary: Vulnerability: a weakness. Exploit: the tool. Threat: someone able and willing. Mitigation: less risk.
Risk combines likelihood and impact; describe impact as lost confidentiality, integrity or availability.
Spoofing powers SYN floods, reflection and amplification; the spoofed source is the victim.
ARP poisoning and rogue DHCP put a man in the middle; DAI, DHCP snooping and encryption stop it.
Malware types differ in how they spread; phishing variants differ by target or channel.
Offline cracking ignores lockouts; awareness, training and physical access control complete the program.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new help desk hire the difference between a vulnerability, an exploit and a threat using one real network example, then walk through how ARP poisoning puts an attacker in the middle, which CIA property it breaks, and which layered controls would stop it.

questions.question: Which term describes a weakness, such as an unpatched service or a default password, that could be used to compromise a system?
choices: Exploit
Vulnerability
Threat
Mitigation
questions.explanation: A vulnerability is the weakness itself. An exploit is the tool that abuses it, and a threat is someone with the means and intent to do so.

questions.question: A switch's web interface has a known bug. Match each term to the piece of this scenario it describes.

pairs.right: The bug in the web interface software
A script that sends the malformed request the bug mishandles
An attacker on the guest Wi-Fi who has the script and wants in
Upgrading the image and disabling the HTTP server

questions.explanation: The weakness is the vulnerability, the tool is the exploit, the actor with means and intent is the threat, and anything that lowers the risk is a mitigation.

questions.question: In the CIA triad of confidentiality, integrity and availability, which property does a denial-of-service attack target?
questions.explanation: A DoS attack keeps legitimate users from getting service, which is an attack on availability. It does not necessarily read or change any data.

questions.question: Thousands of infected home computers start flooding one web server at the same moment on a command from a central server. What is this?
choices: A reconnaissance attack
A man-in-the-middle attack
A distributed denial-of-service attack
A buffer overflow attack
questions.explanation: Many compromised hosts (a botnet) attacking one target on command is a DDoS. The distribution across many sources is what makes it hard to block.

questions.question: A web server becomes unreachable for users. The administrator runs the commands below. What attack is most likely underway?
choices: A TCP SYN flood filling the server's table of half-open connections
An ARP poisoning attack redirecting the server's gateway
A port scan looking for open services
A worm copying itself to the server over HTTPS
questions.explanation: Thousands of connections stuck in SYN_RECV from scattered addresses means SYNs arrive but the final ACK never does. The half-open table fills and real clients are refused: a SYN flood, usually with spoofed sources.

questions.question: Why do attackers favor open DNS resolvers and old NTP servers for amplification attacks?
choices: They run on TCP, so the handshake hides the attacker's address
They accept spoofed UDP requests and send replies far larger than the requests
They cache the attacker's address and block the target
They forward requests through encrypted tunnels
questions.explanation: These UDP services answer anyone, with no handshake to defeat spoofing, and a small query can produce a reply many times larger. With the victim's address as the spoofed source, the large replies flood the victim.

questions.question: Which two steps reduce the chance that your network takes part in reflection and amplification attacks against others? (Choose two.)
choices: Do not run DNS resolvers that answer queries from anyone on the internet
Filter outbound packets whose source address is not from your own address block
Increase the MTU on the internet link
Disable spanning tree on access ports
Permit all inbound ICMP so attacks are easier to trace
questions.explanation: Closing open resolvers removes a reflector, and egress filtering stops hosts inside your network from sending spoofed packets at all. MTU, spanning tree and ICMP policy have nothing to do with reflection.

questions.question: Match each attack to its main goal.

pairs.right: Exhaust a resource so the target cannot serve users
Trick an innocent host into sending traffic to the target
Turn small requests into much larger replies aimed at the target
Eavesdrop on or modify traffic between two devices

questions.explanation: DoS exhausts resources directly; reflection and amplification use innocent hosts as unwitting senders (amplification adds a size multiplier); MITM sits in the path to read or alter traffic.

questions.question: A user complains that everything is working but feels slow. You check the user's PC (10.1.1.25), whose default gateway is 10.1.1.1. What does the output suggest?
questions.code:
C:\> arp -a
Interface: 10.1.1.25 --- 0x7
  Internet Address      Physical Address      Type
  10.1.1.1              00-0c-29-aa-bb-cc     dynamic
  10.1.1.66             00-0c-29-aa-bb-cc     dynamic
  10.1.1.80             00-50-56-12-34-56     dynamic
choices: The gateway has two IP addresses configured on one interface
The PC has a duplicate IP address with 10.1.1.66
ARP poisoning: host 10.1.1.66 has claimed the gateway's IP, putting itself in the middle
A DHCP server has run out of addresses
questions.explanation: The gateway IP and another host map to the same MAC, so frames meant for the router go to 10.1.1.66. Combined with traffic still working, that is the signature of an ARP-poisoning man in the middle.

questions.question: A rogue DHCP server on a LAN hands clients valid addresses but lists the attacker's own IP as the default gateway. What does the attacker gain?
choices: Nothing, because clients ignore the gateway in a DHCP offer
A man-in-the-middle position for all traffic that leaves the subnet
Control of the switch's MAC address table
The ability to change the clients' MAC addresses
questions.explanation: Clients send every off-subnet packet to their default gateway, so a fake gateway places the attacker in the path of that traffic. DHCP snooping exists to block exactly this.

questions.question: Staff use public hotel Wi-Fi, where a man in the middle is possible. Which mitigation still protects the confidentiality and integrity of their traffic even if an attacker intercepts it?
choices: Encrypting the traffic with a VPN or TLS
Using a longer SSID
Disabling IPv6 on the laptops
Turning on port security on the office switches
questions.explanation: Encryption makes intercepted data unreadable and lets the endpoints detect tampering. The office's port security does nothing on a hotel network, and SSID length or IPv6 settings do not protect data.

questions.question: Put the steps of a typical targeted attack in the order an attacker usually performs them.
items: Look up the target's domain and address blocks with whois and DNS tools
Ping sweep the address range to find live hosts
Port scan the live hosts to find listening services
Identify an outdated service version with a known vulnerability
Run an exploit against that vulnerable service
questions.explanation: Reconnaissance narrows from public records to live hosts to open ports to specific weak software. Only then does the attacker exploit something.

questions.question: You find the output below in a log of commands run from a compromised guest laptop. What phase of an attack does it represent?
questions.code:
$ nmap -sS 192.0.2.0/28
Nmap scan report for 192.0.2.10
PORT    STATE SERVICE
22/tcp  open  ssh
80/tcp  open  http
443/tcp open  https
Nmap scan report for 192.0.2.12
PORT     STATE SERVICE
3389/tcp open  ms-wbt-server
choices: Exploitation
Amplification
Reconnaissance
Data exfiltration
questions.explanation: A port scan maps which hosts and services exist. Nothing has been exploited yet, but the attacker now knows where to aim.

questions.question: What makes a buffer overflow vulnerability more dangerous than a simple crash?
choices: It always deletes the device's configuration
It spreads automatically to every host in the subnet
It forces the device to send its passwords in clear text
Carefully crafted overflow data can make the program run the attacker's own code
questions.explanation: Overflowing a buffer overwrites neighboring memory. If the attacker controls what gets written, the program can be steered into running injected code. Spreading automatically describes a worm, not the overflow itself.

questions.question: Match each malware type to how it behaves.

pairs.right: Hidden inside software that looks useful and legitimate
Injects itself into other programs and spreads when files are shared
Copies itself across the network through vulnerabilities, no user needed
Encrypts the victim's data and demands payment

questions.explanation: The classic three differ in how they spread: packaged inside software, attached to other code, or self-propagating. Ransomware is defined by what it does once inside.

questions.question: An employee installs a free screen-recording tool from a download site. The tool works fine, but it also quietly installs a backdoor. Which type of malware is this?
choices: Trojan horse
Worm
Virus
Adware toolbar
questions.explanation: Malware packaged inside useful-looking software that the user chooses to install is a trojan horse. A worm would not need the user to install anything.

questions.question: Which two measures most directly limit how far a network worm can spread? (Choose two.)
choices: Patching the vulnerable service on every host promptly
Segmenting the network and filtering traffic between segments with ACLs
Adding a login banner to every switch
Using a longer DHCP lease time
Enabling CDP on all ports
questions.explanation: Worms move by exploiting a vulnerable service, so patching removes the path and segmentation with filtering blocks it. Banners, lease times and CDP do not affect worm propagation.

questions.question: Match each social engineering variant to its description.

pairs.right: Tailored email to a specific group, such as one company's finance team
Phishing aimed at a CEO or other high-profile person
Phishing done over voice phone calls
Phishing done over SMS text messages
Malware planted on a website the targets regularly visit

questions.explanation: The phishing names describe either the target (spear, whaling) or the channel (vishing, smishing). A watering hole waits on a site the victims already trust.

questions.question: A finance clerk receives a call from someone claiming to be the help desk, asking her to set her password to "Temp1234" for a maintenance window. What kind of attack is this?
choices: Social engineering
Pharming
Brute-force attack
Reconnaissance scan
questions.explanation: The attacker exploits trust and helpfulness by impersonating IT. No technical flaw is used; the person is the vulnerability.

questions.question: Attackers learn that engineers at a chip maker often read one small industry forum. They compromise the forum so it serves malware, and only visitors from the chip maker's address range get infected. What is this attack called?
choices: Whaling
Pharming
Spear phishing
Watering hole
questions.explanation: A watering hole attack compromises a site the targets already visit and waits for them. Pharming would redirect name resolution, and spear phishing would send the targets a message.

questions.question: What is the difference between a dictionary attack and a brute-force attack?
choices: A dictionary attack is offline; a brute-force attack is always online
A dictionary attack targets usernames; brute force targets passwords
They are two names for the same attack
A dictionary attack tries entries from a word list; brute force tries every possible character combination
questions.explanation: Dictionary attacks bet that the password is a known word or a leaked password, which is fast. Brute force guarantees a result by trying everything, which can take far longer. Either can be run online or offline.

questions.question: An attacker has already stolen a file of password hashes. Which two factors most affect how long the offline cracking will take? (Choose two.)
choices: The length and character variety of the original passwords
How slow and strong the hashing algorithm used to store them is
The device's account lockout threshold
Whether the login banner warns against unauthorized access
The exec-timeout on the vty lines
questions.explanation: Offline cracking only depends on the size of the search space (length and character set) and the cost of each guess (the hash algorithm). Lockouts, banners and timeouts act on the live login prompt, which an offline attack never uses.

questions.question: Which password is most resistant to brute force?
choices: Cisco123
P@ssw0rd
blue-river-lamp-cactus-42
Admin!
questions.explanation: Length grows the search space exponentially, so a long passphrase beats a short complex one. The other three are short and also appear in common dictionary lists.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of physical access control?
choices: A login banner on every router
Badge readers that log entry to the network closet
An extended ACL on the internet router
WPA2 encryption on the guest WLAN
questions.explanation: Physical access control limits who can physically reach equipment. Badge readers also leave an audit trail of who entered and when.

questions.question: A company sends short monthly reminders that IT never asks for passwords, and also requires every employee to complete a yearly course on the written security policy. Which two program elements are these, in order?
choices: Physical access control, then user awareness
User training, then user awareness
User awareness, then user training
User training, then physical access control
questions.explanation: Ongoing informal reminders are user awareness. The scheduled, formal course on written policy is user training.

questions.question: Why does an attacker with physical access to a router's console port effectively own the device, even if its passwords are strong?
questions.answer: With console access and the ability to reboot the device, the attacker can perform password recovery, bypass the stored passwords and take full control of the configuration. Locking the closet is therefore a network security control.
questions.explanation: Password recovery is designed for people standing at the console. Physical security is what keeps that power in the right hands.

questions.question: In one or two sentences, explain the difference between a reflection attack and an amplification attack.
questions.answer: In a reflection attack the attacker spoofs the target's address so innocent servers send their replies to the target. An amplification attack is a reflection attack where each small request triggers a much larger reply, multiplying the traffic that hits the target.
questions.explanation: Both rely on spoofing the victim as the source. Amplification adds the size multiplier, which is why DNS and NTP have been favorite reflectors.

questions.question: A security team plans layered controls against ARP-poisoning MITM attacks on the office LAN. Which pair combines a switch-level control with an end-to-end one?
choices: Port security and a login banner
Dynamic ARP Inspection and TLS or SSH for sensitive sessions
A longer DHCP lease and NTP authentication
Disabling CDP and enabling PortFast
questions.explanation: DAI drops forged ARP messages at the switch, and encryption keeps data confidential and tamper-evident even if an attacker gets in the path. That is defense in depth. The other pairs do not address ARP poisoning.

questions.question: Which action reduces a router's attack surface?
choices: Adding a longer login banner
Disabling the HTTP server and other services that are not needed
Raising the size of the logging buffer
Changing the hostname to something generic
questions.explanation: The attack surface is every exposed service, port and account. Turning off services nobody uses removes entry points an attacker could probe. A banner, a hostname or a log setting removes nothing an attacker can reach.

questions.question: Attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in a company's VPN gateway, and the vendor has not yet published a fixed software release. What is this flaw called?
choices: A reflection attack
A mitigation
A zero-day vulnerability
A brute-force attack
questions.explanation: A vulnerability that is known to attackers before a fix exists is a zero-day. Until the patch ships, defenders rely on other layers, such as limiting who can reach the gateway and monitoring for exploitation.

questions.question: Match each incident to the part of the CIA triad it violates.

pairs.left: An attacker captures a Telnet session and reads the password
pairs.right: Confidentiality

pairs.left: A man in the middle changes the account number in a payment
pairs.right: Integrity

pairs.left: A SYN flood stops the web server from answering customers
pairs.right: Availability

questions.explanation: Reading data breaks confidentiality, changing it breaks integrity, and stopping service breaks availability. Naming the property first often points straight at the right control.

questions.question: Which two are examples of least privilege? (Choose two.)
choices: Help desk accounts can run show commands but cannot enter configuration mode
The guest VLAN can reach the internet but no internal subnets
Every engineer uses one shared admin account so nobody is locked out
All users get local administrator rights to cut support calls
The core switch accepts SSH from every subnet
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the access a role needs: read-only commands for the help desk, internet-only access for guests. A shared admin account, admin rights for everyone and SSH from anywhere all grant more than needed.

questions.question: In a DNS amplification attack, each 60-byte spoofed query makes a resolver send a 3,000-byte reply to the victim. What is the amplification factor?
questions.explanation: 3,000 divided by 60 is 50, so every byte the attacker sends becomes 50 bytes at the victim. That multiplier is why attackers abuse open resolvers instead of flooding the victim directly.

questions.question: G0/0 is R1's internet-facing interface. Based on the output, what are lines 10 to 30 of OUTSIDE-IN protecting against?
questions.code:
R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is OUTSIDE-IN
R1# show ip access-lists OUTSIDE-IN
Extended IP access list OUTSIDE-IN
    10 deny ip 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any (1532 matches)
    20 deny ip 172.16.0.0 0.15.255.255 any
    30 deny ip 192.168.0.0 0.0.255.255 any (87 matches)
    40 permit ip any any (982210 matches)
choices: Packets arriving from the internet with spoofed private source addresses
Inside users browsing to websites that use private addresses
Worms spreading between internal VLANs
Brute-force logins on the vty lines
questions.explanation: Private (RFC 1918) source addresses can never legitimately arrive from the internet, so packets carrying them inbound are spoofed, often as part of floods or reflection. The counters show such packets do arrive. The ACL is inbound on the internet link, so it does not see internal VLAN traffic.

questions.question: A company's web server suddenly receives thousands of TCP SYN-ACK segments per second from hundreds of different internet servers, yet it never sent any SYNs to them. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The server is running a port scan against those servers
A worm on the server is opening connections by itself
The servers are performing a man-in-the-middle attack
An attacker is sending SYNs to those servers with the web server's address spoofed as the source, reflecting the replies onto it
questions.explanation: Each reflector answers a SYN with a SYN-ACK to whatever source address the SYN carried. Spoofing the victim's address turns many innocent servers into a flood aimed at the victim, which is a reflection attack. The victim never initiated anything, which rules out a scan or a worm on the server.

questions.question: Put the steps of an ARP-poisoning man-in-the-middle attack in order.
items: The attacker sends unsolicited ARP replies saying the gateway's IP is at the attacker's MAC
Hosts overwrite the gateway entry in their ARP caches
Hosts send their off-subnet frames to the attacker's MAC address
The attacker copies the traffic and forwards it to the real gateway
questions.explanation: Gratuitous ARP replies poison the caches, so the hosts' frames go to the attacker, who forwards them on so nothing appears broken. Dynamic ARP Inspection stops the first step.

questions.question: Ransomware encrypts a company's file shares. Which measure, put in place beforehand, lets the company recover without paying?
choices: A longer DHCP lease time
Offline, regularly tested backups of the data
A message-of-the-day banner on the file server
Disabling CDP on the switches
questions.explanation: Backups that the ransomware cannot reach (offline or immutable) let the company restore the data, which turns a disaster into an inconvenience. The other options do nothing for encrypted files.

questions.question: A stranger carrying boxes follows an employee through a badge-controlled door without badging in. What is this called?
choices: Vishing
Pharming
Tailgating
Whaling
questions.explanation: Following someone through a secured door is tailgating, a physical form of social engineering that relies on politeness. Awareness training and physical controls such as turnstiles or guarded entrances mitigate it.

questions.question: A router refuses all logins for two minutes after five failed attempts. Which attack does this slow down?
choices: Online password guessing at the login prompt
Offline cracking of hashes taken from a stolen configuration
A phishing email that collects the password
Pharming that redirects users to a fake site
questions.explanation: Lockouts and delays act only on the live login prompt, which is where online guessing happens. Offline cracking never touches the device, and phishing or pharming steal the password without guessing at all.

questions.question: Two users happen to choose the same password. Why does salting the stored hashes help against an attacker who steals the hash file?
choices: The salt encrypts the hash so it cannot be read at all
Salting makes the hash reversible for administrators only
Each hash includes a different random value, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables do not work
The salt locks the account after several wrong guesses
questions.explanation: A salt is random data stored with each hash. Identical passwords no longer share a hash, and a precomputed (rainbow) table built without the salt is useless, so the attacker has to crack every password separately. A salt is not secret and does not encrypt anything.

questions.question: Match each attack to the control designed to stop it.

pairs.left: Rogue DHCP server on an access port
pairs.right: DHCP snooping

pairs.left: Forged ARP replies claiming the gateway's IP
pairs.right: Dynamic ARP Inspection

pairs.left: Thousands of fake source MACs on one port
pairs.right: Port security

pairs.left: Eavesdropping on traffic between two offices over the internet
pairs.right: Site-to-site IPsec VPN

pairs.left: Offline guessing of a captured Wi-Fi handshake
pairs.right: WPA3 with SAE

questions.explanation: Each control sits where its attack happens: DHCP snooping and DAI on the access switch, port security per port, IPsec on the WAN path, and SAE in the wireless key exchange.

questions.question: An attacker phished a network engineer's username and password and now tries to log in to the core switch with SSH. Which single control would most directly stop the login even though the password is correct?
choices: service password-encryption
MFA enforced by the AAA server for device logins
A longer exec-timeout on the vty lines
A login banner warning against unauthorized access
questions.explanation: With MFA the attacker also needs the second factor, such as a push approval on the engineer's phone, so a stolen password alone fails. Type 7 encryption, timeouts and banners do nothing against a correct password.

questions.question: What is defense in depth, and why is it needed? Give one example.
questions.answer: Defense in depth layers several independent controls so that when one fails or is bypassed, the others still protect the asset, because no single control stops every attack. Example: a phished password is still blocked by MFA, and an attacker who does get in is limited by ACLs and recorded by accounting logs.
questions.explanation: Exam scenarios often have more than one correct-sounding control; the layered view explains why networks use them together.

questions.question: Cisco publishes an advisory: crafted HTTP requests can trigger a buffer overflow in the IOS web server. Which two actions mitigate it? (Choose two.)
choices: Upgrade to an IOS release that fixes the bug
Disable the web server with no ip http server if nobody uses it
Enable service password-encryption
Add a banner motd
Increase the exec-timeout on the console
questions.explanation: Patching removes the vulnerability, and turning off an unused service removes the path to it until you can patch. Password encryption, banners and timeouts do not affect a flaw in the web server.

questions.question: A vulnerability scan finds two problems: an unpatched web server on an isolated lab VLAN with no route to the rest of the network or the internet, and a fully patched internet-facing VPN gateway whose admin account still uses a default password. Which should be fixed first, and why?
choices: The lab server, because unpatched software is always the highest risk
Both are equal, because each is a vulnerability
The VPN gateway, because it is exposed to the internet and the default password is easy to exploit, so both likelihood and impact are high
Neither, because no exploit has been seen yet
questions.explanation: Risk weighs likelihood and impact. Default credentials on an internet-facing gateway are trivial to exploit and give access to the whole network. The isolated lab server is hard to reach, so its likelihood is low. Waiting for an exploit to appear is not risk management.
